newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-BHP wants economic problems tackled.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-BHP wants economic problems tackled.

text.p: Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd chief executive John Prescott said the Australian government needed to move faster in tackling the economy's major problems, the Courier Mail newspaper reported.

"We won't have to put the brakes on growth like we have in the past. We can sustain higher growth and improve production. But I'm not optimistic it will happen quickly," Prescott said in an interview with the newspaper.

"It (higher growth) is clearly in the government's focus but it will require additional planning and a more co-ordinated effort. They have been concentrating on other things but they need to concentrate on the balance of payments," he said.
Australia's balance of payments would be the biggest issue this year, determining the economy's growth rate, employment prospects and Australia's overall global position, he said.
The November current account deficit of A$1.92 billion, released on Monday, was the highest in 12 months and led to renewed fears that the deficit could again become a negative factor for investors.
Prescott also said his goal for BHP in the current 1996/97 year was to achieve a better return on capital with the emphasis on short-term performance and long-term growth.
"I don't think this will happen without working for it more effectively than in 1996 - getting better at what we're doing and thinking things through."
He said 1995/96 had not been a good year for BHP but there were good indicators for improvement in the current year.
Greater emphasis would be placed this year on quality of BHP employees through a management training college, he said.

BHP had many new investments in the development stage, including a platinum mine and refinery in Zimbabwe, steel works in the United States, Malaysia and Thailand and a diamond project in Canada, Prescott said.
There was also continuing involvement in copper as well as iron projects in Queensland and Western Australia, he said.
BHP, the largest company in Australia in terms of market capitalisation, last month reported a sharp fall in 1996/97 first half earnings.
Net earnings fell by 9.8 percent to A$790 million in the six months to November 30 while operating profit fell to A$1.335 billion from A$1.513 billion.
